title: Mexico’s Federal and Jalisco Governments Will Invest 25 Billion Pesos to Solve the Water Problem in Guadalajara
author: Alonso Urrutia and Alma E. Muñoz
content:
_This article by[Alonso Urrutia and Alma E.
Muñoz](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Alonso%20Urrutia%20y%20Alma%20E.%20Mu%C3%B1oz.)
originally appeared in the [October 28, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/28/politica/gobierno-
federal-invertira-14-mil-millones-y-el-de-jalisco-10-mil-200-millones-para-
suministrar-agua-limpia-en-guadalajara), Mexico's premier left wing daily
newspaper._

With Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus present at the National Palace, President
Claudia Sheinbaum announced that the federal government will invest **14
billion pesos** to address the problem of water supply to the Guadalajara
metropolitan area. With this allocation, the state government will avoid
taking on public debt to finance the project.

In parallel, the governor announced an investment of **10.2 billion pesos** by
the state government so that, jointly, the Chapala-Guadalajara and Calderón-
San Gaspar aqueducts will be built, with which, he said, the problem of water
supply and quality for Guadalajara can be solved at its root. He described
this project as historic for remedying a problem that is decades old and for
reducing water extraction from Chapala.

Lemus highlighted that these investments come from budget adjustments, so, he
assured, there will be **no debt or privatization**. Nor will there be an
increase in water rates for the Guadalajara metropolitan area.

For his part, the head of the National Water Commission, Efraín Morales, said
that the federal government will invest 9.3 billion pesos to build a new
42-kilometer aqueduct, and the capacity of the water purification plant will
be expanded.

In parallel, 5.2 billion pesos will be invested and a second aqueduct will be
built, which will be complemented by the state government's investments in
water sanitation and the closure of illegal discharges, which will be remedied
with the construction of collectors.

During her press conference, the president explained that as an alternative to
confront this water situation in Guadalajara, Lemus had proposed a financing
scheme through public debt, given his government's insufficient public
resources to finance it. Given this situation, together with the National
Water Commission, they opted for a joint investment between both governments.

![El Zapotillo dam](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/02-el-zapotillo-dam.jpg)After the announcement, the
President highlighted that the project will complement the construction of the
El Zapotillo dam (pictured), carried out by the government of Andrés Manuel
López Obrador. Photo: Cuartoscuro / archive

Explaining the actions the state government will carry out, Lemus said that
together, both governments will invest **25 billion pesos** to solve the water
problem in Guadalajara.

He said that with state investment "we will renovate the water purification
plant in Miravalle, which supplies 42 percent of Guadalajara's residents and
is already 70 years old." In a first stage, the aim is for it to begin
operating within six months to supply clean water at 3,000 liters per second.
The three phases, over two years, will involve 7.5 billion pesos in state
funds.

> It is important to finish in six months, because service cuts are being
> experienced, it is necessary to recover flows and overcome the rationing of
> water in their neighborhoods.
>
> Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus

He reported that they will build a network of collectors to prevent the water
coming from Chapala from arriving contaminated, stopping discharges through
the collectors. He asserted that in collaboration with Conagua they detected
**150 illegal water discharges** , both residential and industrial, which are
being closed, and sanctions are being imposed.

Meanwhile, via a link to the border between Nayarit and Jalisco (near Puerto
Vallarta and Bahía de Banderas), the Secretary of Infrastructure,
Communications and Transportation, Jesús Esteva, inaugurated a new highway
section and the Amado Nervo bridge in those states, which would relieve
vehicle traffic in both states, benefiting 480,000 inhabitants of the region
and reducing travel times by up to 40 minutes.
